video_title: What's Behind the Big Surge in US Government Bond Yields | Odd Lots
gist: Recorded at Jackson Hole, Stanford economist Darrell Duffie tells Odd Lots that the surge in long-end Treasury yields is mainly a supply-and-marginal-buyer story (debt/GDP near 100%, the market growing from ~$18T to ~$31-32T in a decade while foreign central banks stay flat) rather than an inflation story, that Treasury Secretary Bessent's expanded buyback program looks more like yield-level signaling than a genuine liquidity fix, and that the Fed's ambition to shrink its balance sheet is constrained because interest-bearing bank reserves have become a 'Swiss army knife' banks won't give up.

themes.theme: Term Premium as a Supply Signal

insights.claim: The term premium is real and measurable in aggregate (it's the gap between long-term yields and the market's expected path of short-term rates), but decomposing it into inflation expectations versus a pure risk/compensation component is genuinely hard, and economists like John Cochrane have done leading work on that decomposition.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Treat 'term premium' as a real, tradeable signal of supply/demand imbalance in duration, not just an academic fudge factor — it rises specifically when Treasury issuance volume rises without credible deficit reduction.
insights.quote: So it tells everyone the value of short term versus long term money and interest rates, but then decomposing it is the hard part.

insights.claim: The term premium rises over time specifically as a function of the volume of Treasury issuance, and it elevates the whole curve more at the long end when investors don't believe fiscal deficits will come down.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: A rising term premium is a real-time market vote on fiscal credibility — persistent widening at the long end is a signal deficit reduction expectations are deteriorating, not just a rates-cycle artifact.

themes.theme: Who Is the Marginal Treasury Buyer

insights.claim: Duffie's framework for why yields must rise even with no inflation or default risk: foreign central banks already hold what they need and are not adding more, so the marginal buyer of new Treasury supply is discretionary, yield-sensitive money (mutual funds, hedge funds, banks, insurance companies, pension funds) that will only absorb more duration if compensated with a higher yield.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Watch foreign official-sector Treasury holdings as a ceiling, not a floor — with that buyer flat, every incremental dollar of issuance has to be cleared by price-sensitive private investors, structurally pushing term premium and long yields higher as issuance grows.
insights.quote: Foreign investors generally are not keeping up with the size of the bond market.

insights.claim: Despite record Treasury trading volumes, primary dealer balance sheets have more capacity than expected — possibly because capital regulations are effectively less binding or dealers have recapitalized — even though Duffie predicted after March 2020 that dealer balance sheets would clog again.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: A key tail risk (dealer intermediation capacity choking Treasury market functioning, as in March 2020) has not materialized yet, but Duffie flags it as still a live risk to monitor as issuance keeps growing at roughly $2 trillion a year.
insights.quote: Even with massive amounts of trading we're seeing today, the dealers have more space yet.

insights.claim: In March 2020, market dysfunction forced the Fed to step in and support the balance sheets of the largest dealers just to keep the Treasury market moving, and yields jumped and became very volatile during that episode.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: This is the reference case for what a real Treasury market liquidity crisis looks like — useful benchmark for judging whether current buyback/liquidity concerns are genuine or overstated.
insights.quote: The fed had to step in and, dig out the balance sheets of the largest dealers to keep the bond market moving. And bond yields jumped and were very volatile.

themes.theme: Debt Volume, Not Debt/GDP Ratios, Explains the Reversal

insights.claim: The old IMF-style 60%-debt/GDP 'red line' has been repeatedly breached and is no longer a useful warning threshold; US debt/GDP is now near 100%, up from well under that a decade ago, and the Treasury market has grown from about $18 trillion to roughly $31-32 trillion over that same ten-year period, rising at about $2 trillion a year.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Debt/GDP ratios have lost predictive power as a yield signal; the more actionable metric is the absolute pace of net new Treasury issuance relative to who is willing to absorb it.
insights.quote: So what's changed is the sheer volume of government debt relative to GDP.

insights.claim: The Japan precedent — where analysts predicted higher yields from high debt/GDP for years while yields kept falling, only to reverse recently — shows that debt-load warnings can stay wrong for a long time before suddenly becoming right, once the sheer volume of debt overwhelms available demand.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal / Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Don't dismiss the 'debt matters eventually' thesis just because it has been wrong for years — Japan shows the regime can flip once volume crosses a threshold, a template investors should watch for in the US.

themes.theme: Hyperscaler Debt Is Not the Real Crowding-Out Story

insights.claim: Contrary to a popular narrative that AI hyperscalers' bond issuance is crowding out Treasuries, Duffie argues the causality runs the other way — Treasury's own issuance volume (roughly $32 trillion outstanding and rising ~$2 trillion/year) dwarfs and is piling onto the same pool of duration-buying capital that hyperscaler debt draws from.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Reframes a popular 'AI capex bond binge is pushing up rates' narrative — the dominant duration-supply story is sovereign issuance, not corporate hyperscaler debt, which is expected to reach only about $1 trillion in the next couple of years, small next to Treasury's scale.
insights.quote: I wouldn't describe it as the hyperscalers crowding out the Treasury Department, but rather the other way around the volume.

insights.claim: All large issuers — sovereign and corporate — are competing for the same finite pool of yield-sensitive discretionary capital (pension funds, insurance companies), so growth in any large duration issuer (hyperscalers, other governments) adds to the same 'piling on' effect pushing yields up across the bond market, even though Treasury remains the dominant driver.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Investment-grade corporate credit spreads and Treasury yields are linked through a shared duration-buyer base — a glut in one segment (e.g., hyperscaler bond issuance) can spill into the other even without direct substitution.

themes.theme: Bessent's Buyback Program: Signaling, Not a Liquidity Fix

insights.claim: When Treasury Secretary Bessent recently expanded the size of the Treasury buyback program citing liquidity concerns, classical liquidity metrics (bid-offer spreads, market depth, dealer balance sheet health) were actually normal at the time — suggesting his real motive was a belief that yields themselves were simply too high, and he has said explicitly he was 'signaling' that view to the market.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Treat the stated 'liquidity' rationale for buyback expansions skeptically — this instance looks like an attempt at yield-level jawboning by a Treasury Secretary with a trading background, which markets may learn to fade once the signaling nature is recognized.
insights.quote: No, I think we subsequently can concede that while the market reacted quickly to that news, it reversed itself pretty quickly afterwards.

insights.claim: The current expanded Treasury buyback program is small in scale (roughly $4-8 billion) compared to what would be needed to meaningfully move yields — Duffie says a genuinely market-moving intervention could be done 'on the scale of hundreds of billions,' making the current program more of a signal than a lever.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Don't expect the current buyback program size to structurally cap long yields — the firepower deployed so far is roughly a rounding error against a multi-trillion-dollar market, so any yield relief attributed to it is more likely psychological than mechanical.
insights.quote: That could be done on the scale of hundreds of billions, not the mere 4 to 8 billion that the Treasury Department has been speaking about over the last couple of weeks.

insights.claim: Duffie frames the current buyback/signaling effort as a 'micro' version of Operation Twist — conceptually similar to shifting the yield curve's slope by buying long-dated and issuing short-dated debt, but at a scale (a few billion dollars) too small to meaningfully move the needle, unlike the original Fed Operation Twist which occurred in a below-target-inflation environment.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Distinguishes genuine curve-control-style intervention from symbolic gestures — investors should size any future Treasury 'twist' by dollar volume, not by the announcement itself, before pricing in a yield-cap effect.
insights.quote: It feels like a twisty type of operation, but a micro twist, it's the firepower that... a few billion dollars.

insights.claim: If the Treasury tried to defend a specific long-end yield level (e.g., capping the 30-year at a fixed rate by issuing only short paper to fund purchases), it would work better as a level-bound commitment (deterring shorts who'd get burned) than as a fixed-volume program, but it would come at the cost of shortening the average maturity of US debt and making a larger share of the government's interest expense reset with current market conditions day to day — a formula for more interest-expense volatility.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: A hard Treasury 'yield cap' via short-term funding is mechanically possible and could squeeze short sellers, but it trades near-term yield suppression for higher long-run fiscal risk via rollover exposure — a real policy tension to watch if intervention escalates.
insights.quote: That would be a formula for increasing the interest rate expense volatility for the US government because your debt maturity is going to be shorter and shorter.

insights.claim: The original, legitimate purpose of Treasury buybacks (as designed under then-Assistant Treasury Secretary Josh Frost) was to regularly and predictably retire illiquid 'off the run' old notes and bonds clogging dealer balance sheets, replacing them with new liquid issuance — a liquidity-improving, taxpayer-money-making 'buy low, sell high' operation, distinct from using buybacks to target yield levels.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Two very different policy tools share the 'buyback' label — routine off-the-run cleanup (Duffie's research finds this effective) versus opportunistic yield-level signaling (the current Bessent expansion) — investors should not conflate the two when assessing durability of any yield impact.
insights.quote: Let's be regular and predictable and clean up these bits and pieces, make the Treasury market more liquid by replacing those with new liquid treasuries, and implicitly make some money for the US taxpayer. Buy, buy low, sell high.

insights.claim: Duffie considers it legitimate for a Treasury Department to step into a genuinely dysfunctional bond market (as in March 2020) using its buyback program rather than leaving it entirely to the central bank, drawing a direct parallel to the Bank of England's 2022 gilt-market intervention during the Liz Truss crisis, where the UK Treasury indemnified the BoE for losses on the gilts it bought while simultaneously tightening policy.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Provides the template for what a legitimate future US Treasury emergency intervention could look like (Treasury-indemnified purchases distinct from monetary policy) — useful reference point if Treasury market dysfunction resurfaces.
insights.quote: You may remember the Liz Truss budget... the Bank of England faced this dilemma. It was tightening its monetary policy, and at the same time it had to buy gilts.

themes.theme: Governments Are Not Powerful Enough to Beat the Bond Market

insights.claim: Duffie draws a direct historical parallel to the 1992 attack on the British pound (in which Bessent himself had a role while working with George Soros' fund): the UK government simply could not defend its currency peg and should never have tried, burning through its firepower in the attempt — implying the US Treasury similarly cannot forcibly control yields if the market decides otherwise, without taking on major risk.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Sets an implicit ceiling on how much Treasury intervention can actually suppress long yields — if the market pushes toward materially higher yields (Duffie cites 6% as a hypothetical trigger), betting that Treasury can hold the line by force is likely to end like the 1992 sterling defense.
insights.quote: The British government was simply unable to defend the pound, and it should never have tried. It used up a lot of its firepower that way.

insights.claim: If Japan's macro situation deteriorates and the Bank of Japan needs to unload its Treasury holdings, that unwind would add to the existing 'piling on' effect from heavy Treasury issuance and other duration supply, worsening the pressure on both US Treasury market functioning and the US government's interest expense.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway / Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Japanese central bank Treasury holdings are a latent supply overhang risk for US yields — a policy shift or crisis in Japan is a plausible catalyst for a further leg up in long US yields, worth monitoring alongside domestic issuance trends.
insights.quote: If things don't go well in Japan and the Japanese central bank needs to unload treasuries, that would add on to this piling on that we just discussed and caused problems for U.S. Treasury markets.

themes.theme: Fed Avoids Fiscal Dominance, but Its Balance-Sheet Shrinkage Push Is Structurally Hard

insights.claim: The Fed is deliberately avoiding any discussion of yield curve control with the Treasury, informed by the acrimonious 1951 Treasury-Fed Accord — despite its name suggesting agreement, it actually resulted from 'a really, really rough argument,' after which the Fed reluctantly supported the bond market briefly before exiting yield curve control and vowing not to revisit it.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: The historical precedent argues against expecting the Fed to backstop long yields via coordinated yield curve control even under fiscal stress — it will resist fiscal dominance, leaving Treasury largely on its own to manage issuance costs.
insights.quote: People think the word accord means they had they had a good agreement. It actually means they had a really, really rough argument.

insights.claim: The new Fed leadership has launched task forces, including one on the balance sheet (reportedly headed by Jeremy Stein, with Raghu Rajan and Karen Dynan), driven by a concern (per Kevin Warsh's prior G30 remarks) that the Fed's large market footprint creates an appearance of encroaching on fiscal policy, which a smaller balance sheet would help dispel.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: A live Fed balance-sheet task force with named, credible economists signals real near-term possibility of policy change to the Fed's asset composition and reserve levels — a catalyst list investors should track through 2026.

insights.claim: Shrinking the Fed's balance sheet is mechanically constrained on the liability side: the Fed cannot easily reduce the Treasury General Account or physical currency in circulation, leaving bank reserves as effectively the only liability lever — but reserves have become 'sticky' because the Fed now pays a full market interest rate on them (unlike pre-2008) and banks want them for liquidity regulation compliance and payment services.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Meaningful Fed balance-sheet shrinkage is a much harder lift than headlines suggest — banks have no incentive to give up interest-paying reserves, so any real reduction will require new tools or regulatory changes, not just asset runoff (QT).
insights.quote: It's a Swiss army knife for finance. We're not going to give those up easily.

insights.claim: A 2017 Jackson Hole paper by Raghu Rajan (with a co-author) described a 'ratchet effect': every time the Fed expands its balance sheet and adds reserves, banks become dependent on holding more of that reserve asset, and attempts to reduce it cause market volatility that forces the Fed to back off.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Explains why QT has historically stopped short of pre-2008 reserve levels — expect any renewed balance-sheet reduction push to hit the same ratchet resistance and stall well above 2000s-era reserve levels.
insights.quote: Every time the fed increases its balance sheet and adds reserves, the banks get addicted to having more of that extremely useful asset reserves, and they're reluctant to give it up.

insights.claim: Duffie predicts (without inside information) that the Fed's balance-sheet task force will recommend changing the composition of Fed assets — reducing long-term Treasury holdings and replacing them with Treasury bills to reduce the volatility of the Fed's own interest expense, and letting mortgage-backed securities roll off — rather than necessarily shrinking total balance sheet size.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: A shift by the Fed toward T-bills and away from long Treasuries/MBS would itself add to demand at the short end and reduce Fed demand for duration — a technical factor for the Treasury bill and MBS markets to watch for in task-force output.
insights.quote: I predict that they will recommend reducing the quantity of long term Treasury securities that the fed holds and replacing those with Treasury bills in order to reduce the volatility of the Fed's interest expense.

insights.claim: Duffie's own view is that the Fed doesn't necessarily need to reduce its balance sheet size today, but it should develop the tools to be able to do so on its own terms — because without such tools, Congress could corner the Fed politically into expanding its balance sheet against its own judgment, and those tools exist at other central banks but have not yet been built out at the Fed.
insights.speaker: Darrell Duffie
insights.so_what: Fed independence on balance-sheet policy is itself a political risk factor — the absence of shrinkage tools is a vulnerability Congress could exploit, worth watching as a source of future Fed credibility/market volatility.

insights.claim: The US Treasury General Account (the government's operating cash balance at the Fed) is commonly cited as covering only about five days of government expenses — an extremely thin cash buffer relative to the scale of federal spending.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: A five-day expense buffer underscores how reliant the US government is on continuous, frictionless access to short-term funding markets — any disruption to bill issuance or repo markets could create acute cash-management stress quickly.
insights.quote: It covers five days of government expenses or something like that.
